topic: Build your own: networking library & a UI layer on Compose

questions.question: Why model a networking library's request pipeline as a chain of interceptors that each call `chain.proceed(request)`?
options: It forces every request through a single thread in strict arrival order
Each step can change the request, short-circuit, or retry by calling proceed again
It removes the need for a connection pool, since each step opens its own socket
It lets the server decide which of the client's interceptors should run on each call
questions.explanation: Chain of responsibility gives every concern (auth headers, logging, caching, retries) one place to wrap the call. Because each interceptor decides whether and how many times to call `proceed`, it can short-circuit or retry without the others knowing. Threading and connection pooling are separate parts of the design.

questions.question: Your library retries on connection resets. Which requests are safe to retry automatically?
options: Every request, because servers reject duplicate requests by default anyway
Only requests with an empty body, since nothing can be applied twice
Only POST requests, since GET responses are usually served from cache
Idempotent ones like GET, PUT, DELETE; POST only with an idempotency key
questions.explanation: A connection reset can happen after the server has already done the work, so retrying a plain POST can charge a card twice. Idempotent methods produce the same outcome when repeated, and an idempotency key lets the server dedupe POSTs. Servers do not dedupe by default.

questions.question: After a backend outage, every client retries at exactly 1 s, 2 s, then 4 s. Why add random jitter to those delays?
options: It spreads retries out so clients don't all hit the recovering server at once
It makes each retry come sooner, on average, than plain exponential backoff
It lets the client skip the wait entirely whenever the network type changes
HTTP/2 requires it to avoid stream ID conflicts between concurrent retries
questions.explanation: Without jitter, clients that failed together retry together, creating synchronized spikes that can knock the server over again. Randomizing each delay smooths the load. It does not make retries faster on average and has nothing to do with HTTP/2 framing.

questions.question: In a well-designed coroutine networking API, cancelling the caller's coroutine should also cancel the in-flight HTTP call, not just discard its result.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. If cancellation only ignores the result, the request keeps holding a connection, using bandwidth and maybe hitting the server for a screen the user already left. Bridging coroutine cancellation to the underlying call (for example closing the call or stream) frees those resources.

questions.question: Ten parallel requests all get 401 because the access token expired. How should the auth layer handle it?
options: Let each request refresh the token on its own and retry with its own new token
Fail all ten requests and send the user back to the login screen to sign in
One refresh at a time; waiters check if the token changed, then retry with it
Retry all ten with the same expired token after a short fixed delay
questions.explanation: A single-flight refresh behind a mutex stops ten refresh calls racing, which can also invalidate each other on servers that rotate refresh tokens. Requests that queued behind the lock see the token is already new and just retry. Forcing a logout is only right when the refresh itself fails.

questions.question: A cached response has an `ETag`. The cache entry is stale. What should the library send, and what happens if the content has not changed?
options: Send `If-None-Match` with the ETag; on 304, serve the cached body
Put the ETag in `Cache-Control`; the server then always resends the full body
Delete the stale entry and send a plain request, as stale entries are unusable
Send `If-Modified-Since` carrying the ETag; on a 200, keep the old cached body
questions.explanation: A conditional request with `If-None-Match` lets the server reply 304 Not Modified with no body, so the client reuses its copy and saves bandwidth. `If-Modified-Since` takes a date, not an ETag. Throwing stale entries away wastes the validator.

questions.question: Which should your library's retry policy do? Select all that apply.
options: Stop retrying when the caller's coroutine has been cancelled
Retry a non-idempotent POST that has no idempotency key
Respect a `Retry-After` header on 429 or 503 responses
Retry 400 Bad Request responses, since they are often transient
Cap the number of attempts and the total time spent retrying
questions.explanation: `Retry-After` tells you when the server will accept traffic again, and caps stop retries from hanging a screen or draining the battery. Retries must also stop on cancellation. A 400 means the request itself is wrong, so repeating it cannot succeed, and blind POST retries risk duplicate side effects.

questions.question: Why does a design-system button take `content: @Composable RowScope.() -> Unit` instead of `text: String`?
options: Composable lambdas recompose less often than plain String parameters do
Callers can add icons, styled text or a spinner while the button keeps its look
A plain String parameter cannot be localized through string resources
Slot lambdas are required for the button to be exposed to accessibility services
questions.explanation: A slot keeps the component in charge of layout, theming and interaction while the caller decides what goes inside, which avoids a growing list of parameters like `icon`, `iconEnd`, `isLoading`. Strings can be localized fine, and accessibility comes from semantics, not from using slots.

questions.question: `staticCompositionLocalOf` suits theme values that rarely change, because changing it recomposes the whole content under the provider instead of tracking each reader.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. A static local does not track who reads it, which makes reads cheap, but a change recomposes everything in the provider's content. `compositionLocalOf` tracks readers so only they recompose, which is better for values that change often.

questions.question: Which are good API choices for a reusable design-system component in Compose? Select all that apply.
options: Take a ViewModel parameter so the component can load its own data
Accept a `modifier: Modifier = Modifier` parameter and apply it to the component's root
Expose colors through a `ComponentDefaults.colors(...)` function with overridable parameters
Apply the caller's modifier to an inner child so outer padding stays fixed
Hoist state: take `value` and `onValueChange` rather than holding the value internally
questions.explanation: A root-applied modifier, a defaults object for colors and sizes, and hoisted state are the conventions Material components use, and they keep components reusable and testable. Passing a ViewModel couples a UI component to a screen's logic. Applying the modifier to an inner child surprises callers whose size or click modifiers stop affecting the whole component.
